children: 1041 GMT - Speculative buying in gold futures has remained relatively restrained despite a 6.2% price rally during the latest reporting week, suggesting some of the demand may be coming from outside the futures market, Saxo Bank says. Managed-money net length rose just 4% to around 151,000 contracts, says Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo. Silver and platinum recorded even smaller positioning responses despite stronger price gains, while Friday's hawkish remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh subsequently pushed precious metals sharply lower. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

1033 GMT - European gas prices remain vulnerable to renewed spikes as restricted Gulf LNG flows threaten to leave the Northern Hemisphere entering winter without normal Qatari supply, ING says. QatarEnergy has extended force majeure for some buyers into early November, while LNG flows from the Persian Gulf remain significantly restricted, say ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey in a note. The tight supply backdrop leaves the global LNG market particularly exposed as the heating season approaches, they say. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

1016 GMT - Eurozone bond yields rise, adding to previous increases, after the release of flash estimate eurozone inflation data for August. Headline annual CPI rose to 3.3% in August, from 2.9% in July, albeit in line with analyst expectations in The Wall Street Journal's poll. The 10-year German Bund yield hits a new 15-year high of 3.364%. It last trades at 3.362%, up 4.8 basis points, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1016 GMT - U.K. government borrowing costs climb to multi-year highs, putting more strain on U.K. public finances, eToro global market strategist Lale Akoner says. Renewed inflation concerns and fiscal uncertainty ahead of the U.K. budget on October 28 are contributing to rising gilt yields, which come in tandem with a rise in sovereign bond yields globally, she says. U.K. 30-year gilt yields earlier hit 5.904%, their highest in over 28 years, earlier in the session, LSEG data show. Ten-year gilt yields hit 5.255%, highest since 2008. "Higher yields improve income, but pressure mortgages, rate-sensitive shares and government finances." (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0952 GMT - China's travel spending remains a bright spot amid tepid consumer demand, according to BofA Securities in a research note. "More than half of the survey respondents took or booked more overnight trips than last summer," the bank says, citing its own survey. Travel demand was also led by higher-income households, pointing to an uneven recovery, BofA says. Higher airfares following the global energy shock prompted consumers to switch transport modes, choose closer destinations instead of abandoning the trips altogether, the bank says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0942 GMT - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, climb to multi-year highs, mirroring a jump in bond yields globally due to inflation worries as oil prices rise. Uncertainty around U.K. fiscal policy ahead of the budget statement on October 28 is also weighing on gilts, Deutsche Bank Research economists say in a note. The budget could be the biggest gilt test ahead of year-end, they say. A potential sharp increase in government borrowing plans risks causing a painful selloff in U.K. government bonds, they say. U.K. 30-year gilt yields surged to 5.903%, the highest since 1998, LSEG data show. Ten-year gilt yields hit 5.253%, the highest since 2008. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0916 GMT - The latest Bank of England money and credit data shows above-forecast rise in U.K. consumer credit in July, indicating households' resilience, Capital Economics' Ruth Gregory says in a note. Consumer credit rose by 2 billion pounds ($2.71 billion) in July, above the 1.8 billion pounds consensus forecast by economists in a WSJ poll. "This suggests households are willing to offset some of the hit to their real incomes by borrowing more." The data come as yields on 30-year U.K. government bonds rise to their highest since 1998. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0853 GMT - The pickup in inflation in Indonesia is not expected to significantly pressure Bank Indonesia to resume rate hikes, especially as the trade balance returned to a surplus, Barclays economist Brian Tan says in a note. Indonesia's inflation rebounded to 3.19% in August from 2.88% in July, while the trade balance returned to a surplus in July after two consecutive months of deficits. The return of a trade surplus is expected to ease concerns over import-driven growth and rupiah pressure, he says. Bank Indonesia is projected to maintain policy rates on hold through 2026 if rupiah pressures stay contained, while previously anticipated rate cuts in 2027 are no longer expected, he adds. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0848 GMT - U.K. 30-year government bond yields, or gilt yields jump to their highest level since 1998, but this could offer investors attractive carry opportunity, Natixis strategists say in a note. "Curve steepness in the long end reflects structural drivers like quantitative tightening, heavy long-end supply and regulatory change, as much as macro fundamentals, creating carry opportunities at current yield levels," they say. The U.K. budget statement due on October 28, could be a key inflection point as the fiscal watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility, is due to deliver an assessment on fiscal credibility, the strategists say. U.K. 30-year gilt yields climb 10 basis points to 5.886%, having earlier hit 5.893%, their highest since 1998, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0840 GMT - China's new housing reforms could weigh on construction activity, says BofA Securities in a note. It is encouraging that manufacturing activity improved in August from July, BofA points out. "In particular, the notable rebound in new orders suggests a better near-term recovery outlook, likely led by large enterprises," it says. However, construction activity continued to remain weak. BofA says the housing reform announced last week, which requires future residential projects to be sold as completed homes or only after structural completion, could reduce developers' capital turnover. This may further weigh on property-related construction activity in the future, BofA says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0827 GMT - Faster tightening is the BOJ's most immediate response to the increase in JGB yields, Capital Economics says. That can reduce lingering concerns about inflation, but it would probably take a further surge in yields to convince the BOJ to step up bond purchases again. The 10-year JGB yield reached 3% for the first time since 1996, but the move has been less abrupt than at the start of the year. Accordingly, the odds of major financial dislocations are small, says CE's Marcel Thieliant. Soaring yields could stress insurers and pension funds, but higher long-term borrowing costs have limited impact on economic activity as most private-sector debt in Japan consists of loans. And since JGB moves are part of a global selloff, authorities may see attempts to tame yields as futile. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0812 GMT - The Bank of Japan is likely to hike or intervene in the coming weeks, given the yen's underperformance, RBC Capital Markets' Abbas Keshvani says in commentary. The yen has underperformed over the last month, undoing most of BOJ's intervention in recent months. A yen recovery will require an aggressive hiking cycle, but the central bank is unlikely to jeopardize growth in such a manner, he says. "Instead, they will likely hike enough to prevent excessive yen weakness until stability in JGBs next year can usher in a currency recovery," he adds. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)
